primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Metformin-associated lactic acidosis from mitochondrial complex I inhibition
mechanism: At supratherapeutic concentrations, metformin inhibits mitochondrial respiratory-chain complex I, impairing oxidative phosphorylation and promoting lactate accumulation, especially when renal clearance is reduced.
vignette: A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and advanced chronic kidney disease continues taking metformin during an acute illness. He develops nausea, hypotension, and severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with markedly elevated lactate.
lead: Inhibition of which cellular process most directly contributes to this toxicity?
correct: Electron transfer through mitochondrial respiratory-chain complex I
distractors: Electron transfer through mitochondrial complex IV
Beta oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids in peroxisomes
Conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA by pyruvate dehydrogenase only
Oxidative deamination of glutamate in the mitochondrial matrix
distractor_notes: Complex IV inhibition is classically associated with cyanide toxicity rather than metformin-associated lactic acidosis.
Peroxisomal very-long-chain fatty-acid oxidation is not the principal metformin toxicity mechanism.
Metformin affects several metabolic pathways, but direct inhibition of mitochondrial complex I is the best-supported respiratory-chain mechanism in MALA.
Glutamate dehydrogenase is not the primary molecular target responsible for metformin-associated lactic acidosis.
key_expl: Metformin accumulation can inhibit complex I of the mitochondrial electron transport chain. Reduced oxidative phosphorylation favors anaerobic metabolism and lactate production while impaired hepatic gluconeogenesis also reduces lactate utilization.
objective: Identify mitochondrial complex I inhibition as a central biochemical mechanism of metformin-associated lactic acidosis.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Vancomycin binds the D-alanyl-D-alanine terminus of peptidoglycan precursors, sterically inhibiting cell-wall polymerization and cross-linking in susceptible gram-positive bacteria.
vignette: A hospitalized patient with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia is treated with intravenous vancomycin.
lead: Which bacterial target is bound directly by this antibiotic?
distractors: Penicillin-binding transpeptidase active sites
The 30S ribosomal A site
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase
Dihydropteroate synthase
distractor_notes: Beta-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins; vancomycin instead binds the peptide substrate D-Ala-D-Ala.
Aminoglycosides and tetracyclines target the 30S ribosomal subunit.
Rifamycins inhibit bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
Sulfonamides inhibit dihydropteroate synthase.
key_expl: Vancomycin is a glycopeptide that binds D-Ala-D-Ala on nascent peptidoglycan precursors, preventing normal polymerization/cross-linking of the gram-positive bacterial cell wall.
objective: Identify D-Ala-D-Ala as the direct molecular binding target of vancomycin.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Aminoglycosides bind the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit near the 16S rRNA A site, causing misreading of the genetic code and disruption of protein synthesis.
vignette: A patient with severe gram-negative sepsis receives gentamicin in combination with another antibiotic.
lead: Which effect on bacterial translation is most characteristic of gentamicin?
correct: Misreading of mRNA after binding the 30S ribosomal subunit
distractors: Prevention of translocation after binding the 50S subunit
Inhibition of peptidoglycan transpeptidation
Blockade of bacterial DNA gyrase
Competitive inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase
distractor_notes: Macrolides inhibit 50S-mediated translocation; this is not the defining aminoglycoside mechanism.
Beta-lactams impair peptidoglycan cross-linking.
Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase/topoisomerases.
Trimethoprim inhibits bacterial dihydrofolate reductase.
key_expl: Aminoglycosides bind the 30S subunit, especially the 16S rRNA A site, causing incorrect decoding of mRNA and production of abnormal proteins.
objective: Recognize 30S binding with mRNA misreading as the characteristic aminoglycoside mechanism.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Macrolides bind the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit and inhibit elongation/translocation of the growing peptide, suppressing protein synthesis.
vignette: A college student with atypical community-acquired pneumonia is treated with azithromycin.
lead: Which step in bacterial protein synthesis is most directly inhibited by this medication?
correct: Translocation of the growing peptide on the 50S ribosomal subunit
distractors: Aminoacyl-tRNA binding to the 30S A site
Initiation of DNA replication by DNA gyrase
Cross-linking of peptidoglycan by transpeptidase
Reduction of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate
distractor_notes: Tetracyclines inhibit aminoacyl-tRNA entry at the 30S A site.
Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase/topoisomerase activity.
Beta-lactams inhibit transpeptidase-mediated cell-wall cross-linking.
Trimethoprim inhibits bacterial dihydrofolate reductase.
key_expl: Macrolides bind the 50S ribosomal subunit and interfere with peptide-chain elongation/translocation, stopping bacterial protein synthesis.
objective: Identify inhibition of 50S ribosomal translocation as the core macrolide mechanism.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Sequential blockade of bacterial folate synthesis by TMP-SMX
mechanism: Sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase by competing with PABA, while trimethoprim inhibits bacterial dihydrofolate reductase, producing sequential inhibition of tetrahydrofolate synthesis.
vignette: An immunocompromised patient with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
lead: Which pair of bacterial enzymes is inhibited sequentially by this combination?
correct: Dihydropteroate synthase followed by dihydrofolate reductase
distractors: DNA gyrase followed by topoisomerase IV
Transpeptidase followed by autolysin
30S peptidyl transferase followed by 50S translocation
RNA polymerase followed by DNA polymerase III
distractor_notes: Fluoroquinolones target DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV.
Beta-lactams target PBPs/transpeptidation and can promote autolysis, not sequential folate blockade.
Peptidyl transferase is associated with the 50S subunit; this pair does not describe TMP-SMX.
Rifampin targets RNA polymerase; bacterial DNA polymerase III is not the paired TMP-SMX target.
key_expl: Sulfamethoxazole blocks dihydropteroate synthase upstream in microbial folate synthesis; trimethoprim blocks bacterial dihydrofolate reductase downstream. Sequential blockade depletes tetrahydrofolate needed for nucleotide synthesis.
objective: Explain the synergistic antimicrobial effect of TMP-SMX through sequential inhibition of bacterial folate synthesis.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis from impaired bone formation
mechanism: Chronic glucocorticoid exposure reduces osteoblast activity and lifespan, promotes osteoblast/osteocyte apoptosis, and shifts remodeling toward net bone loss.
vignette: A 62-year-old woman has taken prednisone for several years for polymyalgia rheumatica. She develops a low-trauma vertebral compression fracture and markedly reduced bone mineral density.
lead: Which cellular effect most directly contributes to the chronic reduction in bone formation?
distractors: Increased osteoblast proliferation and matrix synthesis
Selective inhibition of osteoclast survival only
Increased osteoprotegerin with suppression of RANKL signaling
Increased intestinal calcium absorption
distractor_notes: Glucocorticoids suppress rather than increase osteoblast activity.
Glucocorticoids can favor osteoclast survival early, but the question asks specifically about reduced bone formation.
Glucocorticoids decrease osteoprotegerin and favor RANKL activity rather than the reverse.
They reduce intestinal calcium absorption rather than increasing it.
key_expl: Long-term glucocorticoids reduce bone formation by decreasing osteoblast function and lifespan and promoting osteoblast/osteocyte apoptosis. This contributes substantially to glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis.
objective: Identify impaired osteoblast function and survival as a major mechanism of glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: IgG autoantibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors block receptor function, promote receptor internalization, and activate complement, reducing functional receptor density at the motor end plate.
vignette: A 34-year-old woman has fluctuating ptosis and diplopia that worsen late in the day. Serum testing detects antibodies against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor.
lead: Which change at the neuromuscular junction most directly causes her fatigable weakness?
correct: Reduced density of functional postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
distractors: Reduced presynaptic acetylcholine synthesis from choline deficiency
Increased presynaptic acetylcholine release at rest
Destruction of voltage-gated calcium channels on autonomic postganglionic neurons
Persistent depolarization of skeletal muscle from excess acetylcholine
distractor_notes: Myasthenia gravis is primarily a postsynaptic receptor disorder rather than a defect in acetylcholine synthesis.
Presynaptic acetylcholine release is not increased as the defining lesion.
Lambert-Eaton syndrome targets presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels at motor nerve terminals, not autonomic postganglionic neurons as stated.
Persistent excess acetylcholine causes a different depolarizing/cholinergic physiology.
key_expl: In AChR-positive myasthenia gravis, autoantibodies damage and reduce postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors through functional blockade, accelerated internalization, and complement-mediated injury, lowering the safety factor for neuromuscular transmission.
objective: Relate AChR autoantibodies to loss of functional postsynaptic receptors and fatigable weakness in myasthenia gravis.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Botulinum toxin inhibition of presynaptic acetylcholine release
mechanism: Botulinum neurotoxin is a zinc-dependent protease that cleaves SNARE proteins in cholinergic nerve terminals, preventing synaptic-vesicle fusion and acetylcholine release.
vignette: Several people develop diplopia, dysphagia, dry mouth, and descending flaccid paralysis after eating improperly preserved food.
lead: Which presynaptic process is directly impaired by the toxin responsible?
correct: SNARE-dependent fusion of acetylcholine-containing vesicles with the nerve-terminal membrane
distractors: Synthesis of acetylcholine from choline and acetyl-CoA
Binding of acetylcholine to postsynaptic nicotinic receptors
Reuptake of acetylcholine from the synaptic cleft
Opening of postsynaptic skeletal-muscle sodium channels independent of acetylcholine
distractor_notes: Botulinum toxin does not primarily inhibit choline acetyltransferase or acetylcholine synthesis.
The postsynaptic receptor is intact; acetylcholine release is impaired presynaptically.
Acetylcholine is terminated mainly by acetylcholinesterase rather than synaptic reuptake, and this is not the toxin target.
The toxin prevents transmitter release rather than directly blocking postsynaptic sodium channels.
key_expl: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins required for docking/fusion of synaptic vesicles, reversibly preventing presynaptic acetylcholine release and producing descending flaccid paralysis.
objective: Identify SNARE cleavage with impaired presynaptic acetylcholine release as the mechanism of botulinum toxin.

outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Tetanospasmin blockade of inhibitory neurotransmitter release
mechanism: Tetanospasmin reaches inhibitory interneurons by retrograde axonal transport and prevents release of GABA and glycine, removing inhibitory control of motor neurons and causing spasticity.
vignette: An unvaccinated man develops trismus, painful generalized muscle spasms, and autonomic instability several days after a contaminated puncture wound.
lead: Loss of release of which neurotransmitters most directly causes the motor findings?
distractors: Acetylcholine and dopamine
Glutamate and aspartate
Norepinephrine and serotonin
Substance P and calcitonin gene-related peptide
distractor_notes: Tetanospasmin does not cause spasticity by blocking acetylcholine and dopamine release.
Glutamate and aspartate are excitatory; their loss would not explain disinhibition with spasms.
Norepinephrine and serotonin are not the principal spinal inhibitory transmitters blocked by tetanospasmin.
Substance P/CGRP are not the key inhibitory interneuron transmitters in tetanus.
key_expl: Tetanospasmin blocks release of GABA and glycine from inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord and brainstem. Loss of inhibition leaves motor neurons relatively unopposed, producing rigidity and painful spasms.
objective: Explain tetanus spasticity through loss of GABA and glycine release from inhibitory interneurons.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Loop-diuretic-induced calciuria from loss of lumen-positive potential
mechanism: NKCC2 blockade reduces ROMK-dependent potassium recycling and the lumen-positive transepithelial voltage in the thick ascending limb, decreasing paracellular calcium and magnesium reabsorption.
vignette: A patient with acute pulmonary edema receives intravenous furosemide. In addition to natriuresis, urinary calcium and magnesium excretion increase.
lead: Which change in the thick ascending limb most directly causes this increase in divalent-cation excretion?
correct: Loss of the lumen-positive transepithelial voltage that drives paracellular calcium and magnesium reabsorption
distractors: Increased expression of distal tubular TRPV5 channels
Increased lumen-positive voltage from enhanced potassium recycling
Direct inhibition of parathyroid hormone secretion
Increased proximal tubular calcium secretion through an active transporter
distractor_notes: Loop diuretics act in the thick ascending limb; increased distal TRPV5 expression would favor calcium reabsorption, not explain the acute calciuria.
NKCC2 blockade reduces potassium recycling and lumen positivity rather than enhancing them.
Furosemide does not cause its calciuric effect by directly suppressing PTH.
Calcium handling in the thick ascending limb is largely paracellular; active proximal calcium secretion is not the mechanism.
key_expl: In the thick ascending limb, NKCC2 uptake and ROMK-mediated potassium recycling generate a lumen-positive voltage that drives paracellular Ca2+ and Mg2+ reabsorption. Loop diuretics abolish this electrical gradient, increasing urinary calcium and magnesium loss.
objective: Explain loop-diuretic-induced calciuria and magnesiuria through loss of the lumen-positive voltage in the thick ascending limb.
